body.en: A *half adder* adds two bits A and B and gives a sum S and a carry C. From the truth table: S is 1 when exactly one input is 1, so S = A'B + AB' = A ⊕ B; C is 1 only when both are 1, so C = A·B. It needs one XOR gate and one AND gate. It is called half because it cannot accept a carry from a previous column.

body.en: To add two n-bit *numbers*, n full adders are chained: the carry out of each column feeds the carry in of the next column to the left (a ripple-carry adder). The first column may use a half adder or a full adder with Cin = 0. The final carry out signals that the sum needs an extra bit (overflow for unsigned numbers). The sum S = A ⊕ B ⊕ C is the odd-parity function of the three inputs.

title.en: Build a full adder from half adders

steps.en: Feed A and B into the first half adder
Take its sum S1 = A ⊕ B and carry C1 = AB
Feed S1 and Cin into the second half adder
Its sum is the final S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin
OR C1 and C2 to give Cout

explanation.en: Two half adders add the three bits in two stages, and an OR gate combines their carries (both can never be 1 together).

tagline.en: Adding binary digits with gates: the half adder, the full adder derived with a K-map, a full adder from two half adders, and ripple addition of multi-bit numbers.

myth.en: A full adder's sum is 1 only when exactly one of A, B, Cin is 1.

truth.en: The sum is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1: one or three. For 1 + 1 + 1 = 11 in binary, S = 1 and Cout = 1. With two inputs, "odd" and "exactly one" mean the same thing, so the half-adder rule gets stretched. With three inputs they differ in the row 111, which is a favourite exam row.

say.en: Half adder: S = $A \oplus B$, C = AB (one XOR, one AND).
Full adder: S = $A \oplus B \oplus C_{in}$, Cout = AB + BCin + ACin.
Full adder = two half adders + one OR gate.
The sum bit is 1 for an odd number of 1s; the carry is 1 for two or more 1s.
n full adders chained carry-to-carry add two n-bit numbers (ripple-carry adder).

narration.en: Many people think: A full adder's sum is 1 only when exactly one of A, B, Cin is 1. Actually: The sum is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1: one or three. For 1 + 1 + 1 = 11 in binary, S = 1 and Cout = 1. With two inputs, "odd" and "exactly one" mean the same thing, so the half-adder rule gets stretched. With three inputs they differ in the row 111, which is a favourite exam row.

problem.en: Show that Cout = AB + BCin + ACin simplifies to AB + Cin(A ⊕ B).

steps.en: Write the minterms of Cout: A'BCin + AB'Cin + ABCin' + ABCin.
The rest: Cin(A'B + AB') = Cin(A ⊕ B).
Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B), which is exactly the two half-adder carries ORed.

narration.en: Show that Cout = AB + BCin + ACin simplifies to AB + Cin(A ⊕ B).

say.en: Show that Cout equals AB plus BCin plus ACin simplifies to AB plus Cin(A ⊕ B).
Write the minterms of Cout: A'BCin plus AB'Cin plus ABCin' plus ABCin.
Group ABCin' plus ABCin equals AB.
The rest: Cin(A'B plus AB') equals Cin(A ⊕ B).
Cout equals AB plus Cin(A ⊕ B), which is exactly the two half-adder carries ORed.
So the answer is Cout equals AB plus Cin(A ⊕ B).

body.en: The sum bit of a full adder is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1; the carry is 1 when the majority (two or three) are 1.
